newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: INTERVIEW-ARBED SEES STEEL PRICES RISING.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ARBED SEES STEEL PRICES RISING.

text.p: Luxembourg steel maker Arbed said on Wednesday it expected steel prices and demand to increase in 1997, adding its order books were already showing an encouraging trend.
"Generally speaking, I think from a demand and price point of view the year 1997 will be better than 1996," Arbed's president Joseph Kinsch told Reuters in an interview.
"As we already see, the order books are showing a much more positive evolution."

Kinsch said demand and prices in heavy long products had already improved at the end of last year and since the beginning of this year there was also strong demand and a positive evolution in the price of flat coated products.

"For the next months it will be possible to proceed to further price increases as demand remains quite strong. We foresee better prices during the rest of the year than we saw at the end of last year or at the beginning of this year."
"I would foresee this improvement from the second quarter onwards - that's not only for heavy long and galvanised products, but also for the other flat products," he said.
In the fourth quarter of 1996 flat product prices mostly remained at the low levels seen in the third quarter, though some galvanised products did already begin to see price rises.
"In flat products...everything is sold already for the first quarter of this year. We are already speaking about the second quarter and there will certainly be a price increase," he said.
Kinsch said that as a whole 1996 had to be considered an "unfavourable" year, especially compared to 1995 when the first half had been very good.

He noted that the steel market was already difficult in the middle of 1995 due to customers building up stocks, while the general economic development was not very favourable in second half of 1995 and all of 1996.
This had had a negative effect on real steel consumption in the European Union and on steel prices.

"Generally, the European Union economies will be better in 1997 than in 1996. Economists forsee an increase in GDP in the European Union of 2.3 to 2.5 percent compared to last year's 1.6 percent," he said.
"There will also be a normal positive evolution in the U.S. economy, which will have a positive (effect)."
He said the recent strengthening of the dollar to European currencies was also welcome.
Kinsch had no comment on 1996 results.

In October, when Arbed announced a first-half loss of 249 million francs, he said the second half would be good, but 1996 as a whole would "not be a brilliant year". In May he had said 1996 would probably be less profitable than 1995.
In 1995 Arbed made net profit of 3.7 billion Luxembourg francs. Steel production totalled 11.5 million tonnes and consolidated turnover amounted to 257.1 billion francs.
